sermons.title: But Now: The Righteousness of God Revealed

lines.text: For different reasons, we can believe that the gospel is good news because we can be saved by Jesus, and that's absolutely true. But the good news, first and foremost, is a showing. It is a display. It reveals to us and to all the cosmos who our God is, and he is righteous. That righteousness is more than just wrath. Far more than just wrath against rebellion. It is righteousness, justice, and grace somehow together at the same time. God is just, but he also justifies. He punishes and he liberates. He upholds his holiness and he cleanses the wicked, bringing them into that holiness.

The righteousness of God is revealed in these and countless like them like you and I, yet believing in our need, believing in Jesus Christ to meet that need, that are justified by his grace as a gift through redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Do you see? Everything, everything has been pointing us to the power of God in Christ. Do you see How the Spirit of God does not want— He won't let us. It's not that He doesn't want us. He won't let us separate our believing from the falling short. It's not a way to sneak in this, like, yeah, but you need to be good too. It's not what He's doing. He's saying you can't be good. But that's where the redemption of Christ rescues us.

We did not know what we were learning as we were going through there. We thought what we were seeing is this is everything that God is going to hammer down. But what we found is this is everything that Jesus Christ would pay for with his life and his death. The righteousness revealed in the gospel and the good news is that God has shown himself to be all glorious. He is the one who at his own expense endured our sin, endures our sin, will endure our sin, our hatred, our venomous hearts. He revealed righteousness— his revealed righteousness shows that he yet remains just. He remains just, but he also frees those who receive his grace, the redemption given in Christ Jesus by faith.

Likewise, The Spirit of God, through his tour that he takes us through fallen history, has revealed the most crucial fundamentals for understanding God's saving power in the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Only when we have exhausted all our energy realizing how big our need really is, how desperate our need is, can we begin to see the power at work in God's act of salvation in Jesus Christ. In seeing that we cannot do it ourselves, though we try. In recognizing our helplessness, though we are certain somewhere down deep we can dig and find a way, we can finally hear the words and know that the adversary who haunts our lives, who corrupts our minds and fills us with fear, not because of us, because of Christ, is doomed.

It is in that context of having fallen short, it is with our deep training and understanding that guilt, understanding of that guilt that we, that we have, are given another light to see the courtroom of God's judgment, to understand his righteousness. In Jesus, that courtroom is not one where we sit in the dock preparing to hear our sentencing. In Jesus, that courtroom is not a tribunal of judgment. It is a courtroom of justification. It is the place where all our sin is in fact weighed. It is measured accurately accounted for. And then, in a majestic wave of grace, undeserved favor, the King of Kings and the Lord of Lords, the one who has the ability to exercise every prerogative ever rightly, he stands and he appeals. Calling us who believe, not his enemy, not those who have destroyed him or caused him suffering. He calls us his own, and he declares that we be made righteous, justified. And suddenly, the room that was carved out for our destruction that was to be the hammer of our demise for all the sin that we have ever done, a rightful payment for our rebellion, becomes the very place of our liberation. The courtroom for our condemnation becomes the courtroom where we are adopted. The place where we are supposed to meet our wrath, we find our redemption.

In the Old Testament, it was the movement when the people recognized— it was a movement for the people to see and have something that displayed to them that the way they have lived before God could not go unnoticed. It required punishment of the highest order. Sin against God, sin against an unimaginable holiness, an unapproachable holiness, requires incalculable payment. Yet what we see here in Jesus is not a merely symbolic gesture of wrath. Jesus is shown and put forward as the propitiation by his blood. God the Son in the flesh took on flesh and so that he himself could lay down his life to satisfy the wrath deserved by all who would believe.

once like a child under the protection of a tutor, the Jews had been graced with the guardianship of a divinely authored law. But now, with the coming of Christ, the need for such guardianship was past. No longer were the Jews alone the children of God. The exclusive character of their covenant was abrogated. The venerable distinctions between them and everyone else, of which male circumcision had always been the preeminent symbol, were transcended. Jews and Greeks, Galatians and Scythians, all alike, so long as they opened themselves to believe in Jesus Christ, were henceforth God's holy people.
